speakwise.title: SpeakWise — Child Speech Recognition Research
subtitles: Building a speech recognizer that keeps the details of what a child says
Researcher & Developer · Independent Speech Research · Patent Pending

paragraphs: SpeakWise started with people close to me. A friend and my younger brother had both faced speech difficulties since childhood. Seeing how those experiences affected their willingness to speak made me want to build something that could help.

My first idea was to make their speech sound smoother. I connected speech recognition, text correction, and voice synthesis, then showed them the prototype. Their reactions made me realize I had spent more time deciding what to change than asking what they wanted.

That changed the direction of the project. I began paying more attention to keeping the speaker’s own voice and giving them control over edits. It also led me to an earlier problem: a recognizer can leave out repetitions and fillers before anyone gets to decide whether to keep them.

My current research looks at recognizing children’s speech more accurately while preserving those details. SpeakWise remains a research project; any use as a therapy tool would need separate clinical testing.

0.title: Prototype: Recognition → Editing → Synthesis
0.intro: The early prototype explored how information changes across a three-stage pipeline:

items.title: Transcribe the speech
items.body: Whisper turns audio into text. I keep the input available because a recognizer can miss words, repetitions, or fillers.

items.title: Choose how much to edit
items.body: An LLM proposes edits, with a correction setting that adjusts how much changes. The original transcript stays separate from the suggestion.

items.title: Hear the revised version
items.body: XTTS uses voice cloning to read the edited text in a version of the speaker’s own voice. The aim is to offer help without replacing their voice.

paragraphs: After getting feedback on the early prototype, I wanted the speaker to have more say in the result. The correction setting λ lets the amount of editing vary instead of applying the same level to every utterance. I wanted to explore how much a system could change while still leaving the speaker in control.
1.title: A Control Over How Much Changes

paragraphs: A quick response is useful, but speech arrives a little at a time. Waiting longer gives the system more context; responding sooner risks acting on an incomplete sentence. I want to test that trade-off alongside recognition and editing errors.
2.title: Timing, Context, and Error Propagation

paragraphs: I filed a U.S. provisional patent application for SpeakWise on August 23, 2026. It covers controllable speech repair, keeping the original utterance, and synthesizing a revised version while preserving the speaker’s voice. The application is patent pending; a provisional filing is not a granted patent.
1.title: Scope and Status

items.body: Systems and Methods for Controllable, Evidence-Preserving Speech Repair with Identity-Preserving Synthesis
items.label: Title

items.body: August 23, 2026
items.label: Filing / Receipt Date

items.body: Ethan Li
items.label: First-named inventor

Interdisciplinary Linguistics Component.heading: What Gets Kept in a Transcript?

0.intro: The project has led me to think about three questions:

items.label: Keeping the details
items.body: A repetition or filler is something we can look for in a transcript. Keeping it gives someone a chance to examine it later.

items.label: Words and meaning
items.body: An edited sentence may read more smoothly but change the original wording. I keep the transcript and the suggested edit separate.

items.label: The bigger picture
items.body: Counting word errors cannot tell me everything about whether an edit kept the speaker’s meaning. That still needs context and human judgment.

paragraphs: What interests me is how a technical choice can change the record of someone’s speech. Keeping a repeated word lets a person examine it later. Removing it takes that choice away. Understanding why the speaker repeated it is a different question.

1.title: What a Useful Speech Tool Must Make Visible
1.intro: Producing fluent text is only one part of the problem:
items: Distinguish the recorded utterance, the recognizer’s transcript, and any proposed rewrite.
Make recognition and editing failures inspectable instead of presenting a polished result as ground truth.
Keep identifiable recordings and child-related data private; public examples require appropriate permission.

paragraphs: The next step is to test how the recognizer works inside the larger application. That means checking speed, privacy, editing quality, and whether users can see and control changes to their speech.
2.title: Application Boundaries

columns.heading: Speech Models
items: Phase 1: Whisper transcription, LLM editing, XTTS voice synthesis
Phase 2: wav2vec 2.0 with CTC
Speaker-separated evaluation; word errors and repetition/filler recall

columns.heading: Application
items: Python backend
WebSocket streaming prototype
Docker deployment

Expected Outcomes & Scholarly Contributi.heading: Questions That Came Out of the Prototype

items.label: Access
items.body: Could a practice interface be easier to reach and use? Accessibility is a design goal, not a demonstrated treatment outcome.

items.label: Agency
items.body: Can a person inspect or reject a revision rather than have their speech silently replaced?

items.label: Evaluation
items.body: How should transcription quality, editing quality, and usefulness of feedback be evaluated separately?

1.title: Questions I Had to Think About
1.intro: Building it raised a few related questions:

items.label: Speech processing
items.body: Check transcription errors and whether repetitions and fillers are kept.

items.label: What the transcript keeps
items.body: Keep a record of what was said separate from an edited version.

items.label: Information quality
items.body: Ask what is lost between audio, text, and synthesized output, and make those losses visible.

items.label: Human-computer interaction
items.body: Treat control over editing and access to the original as interface questions.

paragraphs: SpeakWise received Honorable Mention at the Dallas Regional Science & Engineering Fair and first place at the Highland Park High School SciTech Fair, with a $3,000 award. These recognized the earlier speech-repair prototype.
2.title: Science Fair Recognition

paragraphs: For Phase 2, I adapted wav2vec 2.0 with CTC to children’s speech. The study used 116.0 hours of training audio from 1,738 children (64,941 utterances), then evaluated 17,306 utterances from 434 children kept separate from training.

The manuscript reports a 21.74% word error rate and 69.1% recall for marked fillers and immediate whole-word repetitions. Word error rate counts replaced, missing, and added words; recall measures how many of the marked details the transcript kept. Neither score measures a child’s fluency or a therapy outcome.

I also adapted the recognizer with 3.88 hours of preschool speech from 36 children. On 1,293 paired validation utterances from nine unseen four-year-olds, word error rate fell from 79.31% to 68.95%. Errors remained high, and the small group limits what I can conclude.

These are results reported in the Phase 2 manuscript summarized in the poster above. My sole-authored paper was accepted for presentation at the IEEE BigData 2026 High School Symposium, scheduled for December 17, 2026, in Phoenix.

items.label: Transcription errors
items.body: I used word error rate to count replaced, missing, and added words. It measures transcription mistakes, not how fluently a child speaks.

items.label: Younger speakers
items.body: I looked at younger speakers separately so an overall average would not hide where the model had more trouble.

items.label: Preschool adaptation
items.body: I also tried adapting the recognizer to preschool speech. The small test group makes this an early result that needs more testing.

items.label: Keeping repetitions and fillers
items.body: I checked which marked repetitions and fillers remained in the transcript. The rules for counting them matter when comparing models.

items.label: Research artifact
items.body: The paper, “SpeakWise: Repair-Ready Child Speech Recognition via Verbatim Evidence Preservation,” describes the study. The full methods are needed to make sense of any reported scores.

2.intro: I still need to test how the new recognizer works with the editing and voice-synthesis stages.
items: Validate repair against the preserved original transcript and audio.
Evaluate synthesis fidelity separately from transcription accuracy.
Measure streaming behavior and latency under specified conditions.
Test how users inspect and control proposed revisions.

paragraphs: The hardest lesson came from showing the early version to the people who inspired it. I thought smoother speech would be an obvious improvement. Their reactions made me see that I had not asked enough questions before building it.
I began to separate what I could change technically from what someone actually wanted changed. Keeping their own voice and choosing how much help to use mattered in ways I had overlooked.

That lesson also shaped the recognition study. If a model quietly removes a repetition, the speaker no longer gets to decide what happens to it. I want to make the transcript more accurate without assuming that every detail that sounds different is a mistake.

SpeakWise has taught me to listen before deciding what to build. I want to study language itself alongside the systems that process it: how people express meaning, what a transcript preserves, and which choices belong to the speaker.

pomelo-labs.title: PomeloLabs.ai — AI Search Analytics & Optimization Platform
subtitles: A subscription-based AI marketing platform used by businesses
Founder & Lead Developer · GEO Analytics · Patent Pending

Product Experience & Core User Journey.heading: A Live Product Built for Real Marketing Work

paragraphs: PomeloLabs.ai is a live commercial AI marketing platform with active business users on subscriptions. I built tools to measure how a brand appears across major AI search engines and help a team decide what content to improve.

For one B2B client, AI discovery rate increased from 21% to 63%, as reported in my October 2026 Common App. This is a result for that client, not an average across customers or a promise of the same result for another business.

I developed the software independently, including its architecture, integrations, testing, and deployment. My mother’s company, CrestPoint Marketing, handles marketing and deployed PomeloLabs.ai at OneSource Cloud, an existing CrestPoint client. Her business requirements and agency feedback helped guide the product.
With a live product, the work continues after a feature first runs. Data collection, drafts, permissions, review, and publishing have to work together for the business using them.

1.title: From a Business Question to a Marketing Task

items.title: Add company information
items.body: Start with the business, audience, goals, and source material.

items.title: Review the dashboard
items.body: Look at AI-search results, website data, and planned work together.

items.title: Ask a question
items.body: Direct a question to an agent with the relevant company background.

items.title: Choose a task
items.body: Follow a finding to a proposed task or content brief.

items.title: Review the draft
items.body: Edit the work and approve it before it goes to a publishing channel.

items.title: Follow the results
items.body: Repeat the checks under comparable conditions to see what changed.

items.title: Dashboard / Weekly Plan
items.body: Bring AI-search results, traffic, content, and tasks together to help a team choose its weekly priorities.

items.title: AI Agents / Team Chat
items.body: Four agents share relevant company information and chat history. Users can direct a question to a particular agent.

items.title: Tasks
items.body: Turn a suggestion into an assigned task with a status and a link to the right brand.

items.title: Content
items.body: Create drafts and images, edit them, request approval, and queue work for connected publishing channels.

items.title: Competitors
items.body: Collect competitor website information and track changes for the team to review.

items.title: Keywords / SEO
items.body: Show search intent, volume, difficulty, cost per click, rankings, and possible landing-page topics.

items.title: GEO / AI Search Visibility
items.body: Compare how models describe a brand, follow the results over time, and share a report.

items.title: Settings / Billing / Team
items.body: Manage separate workspaces, team permissions, connected accounts, and Stripe subscriptions.

Motivation.heading: Why I Wanted to Build It

items.label: Scattered information
items.body: Search results, website data, and drafts often sit in different tools. I wanted the relevant information together without losing where it came from.

items.label: Too much to review
items.body: Generating more content does not tell a team which task matters most. The report needs to explain why a task is worth doing.

items.label: Missing background
items.body: A useful recommendation needs the company’s audience, goals, and source material.

items.label: Different kinds of mentions
items.body: A name in a list, a comparison, and a recommendation say different things about a brand.

items.label: Changing answers
items.body: An AI model can answer the same question differently. I use repeated tests to look for patterns.

paragraphs: During development, I pushed back on an early scoring approach that emphasized positive signals. I thought a useful report needed to show where a business was falling short, even when the result was less encouraging.
A brand being mentioned is only part of the picture. I wanted the evaluation to look at how it was described and give the person reading the report a clearer idea of what to do next.
1.title: What a Useful Report Should Show

0.title: Keeping the Steps Connected
0.intro: I built the workflow so a team can follow the information from its source to the action it suggests:

items.title: Save the background
items.body: Keep the company’s audience, goals, and supporting material with its work.

items.title: Collect results
items.body: Bring in search data, website information, and AI answers, with their sources.

items.title: Explain a finding
items.body: Ask the relevant agent to explain what the result may mean for that company.

items.title: Suggest a task
items.body: Create a draft or task that someone can review.

items.title: Get approval
items.body: Use permissions and approval steps before publishing.

items.title: Check again
items.body: Keep the action history and later results so the team can revisit a decision.

items.label: Quality beyond presence
items.body: Look at how a brand is described, including whether the answer is accurate and relevant to the question.

items.label: Clear agent boundaries
items.body: Give each agent a specific job and the company information it needs. I still need to check the answer against its source.

items.label: Keeping the background attached
items.body: Keep the background information attached to the task so someone can understand why it was suggested.

items.label: Human review
items.body: Let a person review work before the system takes an action such as publishing it.

paragraphs: Different teams use the platform, so keeping their information separate matters. Permissions also determine who can review a draft and who can publish it.
I learned to test these steps separately. A model can return an answer successfully while the answer itself is still wrong.
2.title: Reliability Is More Than a Model Score

GEO Evaluation — Product Evolution & Pri.heading: Looking More Closely at AI Answers

paragraphs: I started the evaluation work with a simple question: what should count as a useful mention in an AI answer? Asking a model the same question several times showed why one response is not enough to describe a pattern.

I designed the GEO evaluation framework covered by a U.S. provisional patent application filed on July 27, 2026. The application covers methods for measuring and scoring how a brand appears in AI-generated search answers. It is patent pending, rather than a granted patent.
A product name near the end of a list is different from a clear, accurate recommendation. I wanted the evaluation to capture those differences instead of counting every mention the same way.
The categories need to be clear enough for another person to disagree with a score and explain why. That is more useful to me than a number that simply looks precise.
2.title: A Mention Is Not the Same as a Recommendation

items.title: Detect presence
items.body: Establish whether an answer mentions the entity and retains relevant context.

items.title: Examine the surrounding language
items.body: Evaluate relevance, factual description, and recommendation context against explicit criteria and a defined user question.

items.title: Validate the scoring framework
items.body: Compare scores with human review and look at where people and models disagree. This is work I want to develop further.

paragraphs: I want an evaluation to help someone find a problem they can understand. If a score hides an inaccurate description, it is not doing its job.
The questions we ask and the rules we use to score answers shape the result. I try to keep those choices visible and use consistent conditions when comparing results.
Repeated tests help show how much answers vary. Explaining why a result changed takes more evidence.
4.title: Measurement Should Remain Open to Question

items.body: System and Method for Statistical Measurement, Scoring, and Predictive Optimization of Entity Visibility in Generative Artificial-Intelligence Search Engines
items.label: Title

items.body: Ethan Li
items.label: First-named inventor

paragraphs: The platform works with many kinds of information: a company’s background, what its audience is searching for, drafts, and publishing records. I learned that each needs a clear place in the workflow so the next step has the right context.

A useful workflow should let someone follow the path from a question to a draft and then to an approved action. Keeping context helps, but people also need a way to update it when it is wrong or out of date.
2.title: Context Needs Structure and Revision

items.title: Company Background
items.body: Keep each brand’s audience, products, evidence, and writing preferences together, without mixing information between brands.

items.title: Search Data
items.body: Keep ordinary search performance and AI-answer results distinct so the team knows what each number measures.

items.title: Writing for Different Channels
items.body: An article, newsletter, and social post need different structures. Drafts stay separate from approved and published work.

items.title: Competitor Research
items.body: Connect a change on a competitor’s site to a question the team can investigate, rather than just adding another number to a dashboard.

paragraphs: My work helps connect AI-answer results to tasks and drafts that people can review. I keep generation, review, and publishing as separate steps so a model response does not automatically become a public action.
The challenge is carrying the right information between those steps without making the process confusing for the user.
1.title: What the Implementation Supports

items.label: Uncertainty
items.body: A clear-sounding explanation still needs evidence and a person’s review before publication.

items.label: External failures
items.body: If a connected service fails or a login expires, show the problem and give the user a way to try again.

items.label: Freshness and coverage
items.body: Make it clear when a source has not been checked or its information is out of date.

items.label: Resource use
items.body: Track sampling and generation so repeated requests remain understandable and controllable.

0.title: What the Workflow Is Designed to Support

items.label: Getting started
items.body: Show the background information a user needs before starting a task.

items.label: Following the steps
items.body: Connect observations, drafts, review, and publication.

items.label: Organization
items.body: Keep context associated with the work that uses it.

items.label: Interpretation
items.body: Explain why a result might matter and what still needs checking.

items.label: User control
items.body: Let people inspect and approve work that affects an external audience.

items.label: Defining the score
items.body: The way I define a category changes what a score tells the user. I need to explain those choices clearly.

items.label: Passing context between steps
items.body: Passing work between agents also means passing information. I have to check what gets lost along the way.

items.label: Understanding a change
items.body: A history of actions helps show what happened. Finding out why a result changed takes more work.

items.label: Checking the summary
items.body: A well-written summary should still let someone check the evidence behind it.

paragraphs: The 21% to 63% AI discovery result for one B2B client gave me a concrete outcome to report. I still need to keep each result tied to the client and the way it was measured.

Building a subscription product also meant explaining technical decisions to someone approaching it from the business side. We sometimes disagreed about what a report should show. Working through those differences helped me think about what a customer could actually learn from it.
I learned that defining a score is part of building the product. Someone should be able to see which answers produced the number, find an inaccurate description, and decide what to work on next.
2.title: Building for Paying Business Users

items.label: API scope
items.body: Separate available read and status-management interfaces from proposed automation.

items.label: Product scope
items.body: Describe undelivered reporting and agency capabilities as future work.

items.label: Testing scope
items.body: Use isolated test accounts for integrations and avoid customer data in public demonstrations.

items.label: Outcome scope
items.body: The 21% to 63% AI discovery result is for one B2B client. I need consistent measurements across more clients before describing a broader pattern.

Content drafting, images, editing, approval, and a publishing queue.
Keyword and competitor research, website analytics, and AI-search evaluation.

items: Compare scoring categories with reviewer judgments and examine disagreement.
Keep observations linked to the questions and conditions that produced them.

vla-robot-manipulation.title: VLA Robotics — Learning Robot Manipulation with Vision-Language-Action Models
subtitles: Training and evaluating robot manipulation policies across tabletop and lightbox environments
Research Team Leader · UT Dallas STEM Bridge Program · 3rd Place of 20+ Teams

Motivation & Research Value.heading: Researching Robot Learning at UT Dallas

paragraphs: I joined the six-week UT Dallas STEM Bridge program and led a five-person team studying vision-language-action models for robotic arms. We worked with graduate mentors and faculty at the Intelligent Robotics and Vision Lab.

Our work included training and testing policies, preparing a research poster and presentation, and demonstrating the robot live. The project placed third among more than twenty teams. The hardware and experiments were shared team work.
0.title: My Role in a Collaborative Study

paragraphs: The project looked at how a robot uses a camera image and an instruction to choose an action. One example was picking up bread and placing it on a red plate.
We compared how policies worked in tabletop and lightbox settings, including what happened when the training environment and test environment were different.
A demonstration includes more than the motion we want the robot to learn. It also includes the background and lighting. Changing the scene helped us ask which details the policy was relying on.
2.title: Why the Data Distribution Matters

Data Collection & Model Training.heading: Collecting Data and Training the Policy

paragraphs: We used a leader arm to guide a follower arm and recorded what the camera saw alongside the arm’s actions. We then trained SmolVLA and tested it on the real arm. As team leader, I helped coordinate the steps and keep the experiment moving.

The poster compares pretrained π0.5 and SmolVLA policies on VLARePlica tasks. We then used SmolVLA for the tabletop and lightbox experiments. These comparisons describe our particular tasks and test conditions.

1.title: Policy Comparison — Read With the Poster Protocol

items.label: π0.5
items.body: The reported comparison favored this policy under the poster’s specific conditions, not across robotics settings generally.

items.label: SmolVLA
items.body: The team selected this policy for further experiments within available resources. Model choice and environment transfer are separate questions.

paragraphs: For one task, the robot had to pick up bread and put it on a red plate. We compared policies trained with tabletop demonstrations, lightbox demonstrations, and a mixture of both. The poster gives the trial setup needed to interpret the results.
2.title: A Fixed Task Under Different Conditions

items.label: Tabletop → Tabletop
items.body: The poster reports stronger performance when training and execution matched.

items.label: Tabletop → Lightbox
items.body: Moving to a different scene reduced success in the reported runs.

items.label: Merged → Tabletop
items.body: Combining demonstrations improved the observed cross-condition behavior.

items.label: Merged → Lightbox
items.body: Mixed-condition training also improved behavior in the lightbox relative to single-condition transfer.

items.label: Lightbox → Tabletop
items.body: The reverse transfer exposed a similar sensitivity to scene changes.

items.label: Lightbox → Lightbox
items.body: Success in a matching environment did not establish robustness outside it.

items.label: Matching conditions can conceal brittleness
items.body: Doing well in the training setup does not tell us enough about how a policy will do somewhere else.

items.label: Data diversity is a useful intervention
items.body: Using demonstrations from both conditions helped in our tests. I would want more experiments before drawing a broader conclusion.

items.label: Other explanations remain possible
items.body: We changed several scene details at once. Further tests could separate the effects of lighting and background.

paragraphs: As research team leader, I helped coordinate the work from data collection through training and testing. I also worked with the team on the poster, presentation, and live demonstration. The results came from our combined work and the guidance of our mentors.
1.title: My Contribution and the Team’s Work

items.label: The examples we collect
items.body: Each demonstration records what the camera sees and how the arm moves. The examples we collect affect what the policy learns.

items.label: Words and objects
items.body: The instruction refers to objects in a real scene. I found it interesting to see how words, images, and actions have to work together.

items.label: Evaluation
items.body: Showing the test conditions and failures helps another person understand what the result really says.

paragraphs: This was experience working through a research process with a team: collect demonstrations, train a policy, test it, and decide what to try next. I also had to help explain the work in a poster, a presentation, and a live demonstration.

Our tests showed why it mattered to change the environment instead of judging the policy only where it had trained. The mixed-condition experiments gave us another approach to compare. I learned to pay attention to the background and lighting as well as the task we wanted the robot to complete.
I learned to keep a result tied to the conditions we tested. Working with teammates and mentors also gave me practice explaining an approach, listening to suggestions, and revising it.

items: Try more tasks, objects, and scenes, with repeated trials for each condition.
Change lighting and background separately to see which affects the policy.
Compare training cost, response speed, and task success across policies.
Test whether more varied demonstrations help the robot handle unfamiliar scenes.

expressive.title: Expressive — Open-Source Audio Plugin
subtitles: An open-source audio plugin I built with C++ and JUCE
Independent Developer · C++ / JUCE · Open Source

Motivation.heading: From Making Music to Making a Plugin

paragraphs: Expressive grew out of my own music production. I have played piano and clarinet, and this project gave me a way to bring programming into that part of my life. I built an effect that uses MIDI note velocity to move a sound across the stereo field.
I developed the plugin independently with C++ and JUCE, learning how to make it work inside existing music-production software. I then released the code so other people could try it and change it.
By my October 2026 Common App, Expressive had reached 3,400+ downloads from producers and 40+ GitHub stars. Downloads and stars describe its reach; they are not counts of active users.

items.title: Read the performance input
items.body: A MIDI note-on message includes a velocity value. The plugin maps that value to a position between left and right.

items.title: Smooth the transition
items.body: The sound moves toward the new position over a chosen interval, which helps avoid abrupt jumps and clicks.

items.title: Render the spatial change
items.body: Equal-power panning sets the left and right levels. I also added a choice between working from a mono sum and balancing the existing stereo signal.

1.title: Controls as Choices About the Mapping

items.title: Smoothing Time
items.body: How quickly should a change in playing dynamics become a change in stereo position?

items.title: Pan Width
items.body: How strongly should velocity affect movement? A narrower range keeps the effect subtler.

items.title: Pan Curve
items.body: How should velocity differences be distributed across stereo space?

items.title: Mono Collapse
items.body: Should the tool reposition a mono sum or preserve more of the existing stereo relationship?

1.title: Release, Reach, and What I Learned
items: I built the VST3 audio effect and its panning controls in C++ with JUCE, then released it as open-source software.
Reported in October 2026: 3,400+ downloads from producers and 40+ GitHub stars.

I learned C++ and how to make a plugin work inside the tools music producers already use. Adjusting the smoothing, panning range, and controls changed what I heard. I had to think about how another musician would choose those settings too.

Taking a personal music idea through to a working release gave me practice finishing software that other people could download and try. The standalone build also lets someone test the effect without a DAW.

activityhub.title: ActivityHub — Volunteer Coordination
subtitles: Helping volunteers and organizers keep track of events and service hours
President of Computer Science Chapter · ACAESUSA · Independent Developer

Motivation.heading: Building for a Community I Help Lead

paragraphs: Through ACAESUSA (Asian Culture and Education Society USA), I volunteered at fundraisers and events, taught computer-science skills to members, and served as president of its Computer Science Chapter. I built ActivityHub in 2026 to help the organization manage events, volunteer registration, attendance, and service hours.

I designed and developed the platform myself. Volunteers can submit hours and supporting documents; administrators can approve them or return them for corrections. I wanted both groups to have a clear place to see what needed attention.

How It Works.heading: From Signing Up to Confirmed Hours

0.title: From Registration to a Service Record

items.title: Publish an event
items.body: Administrators publish event details and any supporting copy or posters.

items.title: Register a participant
items.body: Volunteers sign up or join a waitlist. Attendance is recorded separately.

items.title: Collect a check-in
items.body: Volunteers check in with a QR code or event code so an organizer can review attendance.

items.title: Confirm hours
items.body: Administrators review and confirm hours. Repeating the action must not create duplicate credit.

items.title: Produce a record
items.body: Approved hours can be exported or included in certificates. Organizers remain responsible for confirming eligibility for service awards.

items.title: Volunteers
items.body: View registrations and records, submit supporting documents, and understand how to correct a returned submission.

items.title: Administrators
items.body: Review evidence, confirm hours, and make adjustments with a traceable reason.

items.title: Multiple Organizations
items.body: Keep membership, roles, and records within the organization authorized to access them.

items.title: Bilingual & Mobile
items.body: Users can switch between English and Chinese and access the platform on a phone.

items.label: Separate events from records
items.body: An organizer can update an event without silently changing someone’s past service record.

items.label: Avoiding duplicate records
items.body: Repeated clicks or requests should not reserve an extra place or count the same hours twice.

items.label: Checking permissions
items.body: The database checks who is allowed to read or change each record. Hiding a button alone is not enough.

items.label: Keeping a history
items.body: A history of changes and the reason for an adjustment help people work out how a record changed.

items.label: Keeping documents private
items.body: Supporting documents stay private, with links that expire after a short time.

paragraphs: ActivityHub asked me to think about two different sides of the same process. Organizers need to check attendance and records. Volunteers need to submit their hours, fix missing information, and get a record of their service.

I learned to work through the everyday details, including what happens when a submission is incomplete and how someone can correct it. Those steps matter just as much as getting a sign-up form to work.

The platform also supports separate organizations, each with its own members and records. I had to think through who could see a record, who could change it, and how someone would know that their hours had been approved.

zeitgeist.title: Zeitgeist — AI-Assisted Stock Market & Investment Research
subtitles: Organizing stock market data for investment research
Founder & Developer · Stock Market & Investment Research

Motivation & Societal Need.heading: An Independent Project in Market Data and AI

paragraphs: I built Zeitgeist to bring stock-market research into one place: market data, deep-research stock analysis, and interactive CFO insight agents that let a reader ask follow-up financial questions.
As founder and developer, I built the data collection, FastAPI backend, and AI integration. I wanted readers to be able to tell a reported number from a calculation or the model’s explanation of it.

By my October 2026 Common App, the site had received 1,000+ clicks in Google Search Console. These are search clicks, not a count of users or a measure of investment performance. The platform is for research and education, not personalized investment advice.

items.label: Uneven access
items.body: Readers have different tools and background knowledge; an interface should not assume expertise.

items.label: Information overload
items.body: Combining streams is helpful only if their meanings and relevance remain distinguishable.

items.label: Framing effects
items.body: The wording of a summary can encourage confidence beyond what the data supports.

items.label: Domain vocabulary
items.body: Terms such as volatility and delta need explanation without losing technical meaning.

paragraphs: I want readers to be able to tell which statements come from data, which come from calculations, and which are the model’s interpretation. This is a research and educational prototype, not personalized investment advice.

0.title: From Market Data to a Written Summary
0.intro: I had to check different things at each step:

items.title: Collect observations
items.body: Use market API responses as source data. Timestamps, coverage, and delays depend on the provider and cannot be inferred from a fluent summary.

items.title: Structure the information
items.body: Organize inputs and calculated measures into fields the application and model can interpret.

items.title: Generate an explanation
items.body: Ask the model to explain the supplied data, then check its statements against the inputs.

items.title: Present a research summary
items.body: Return an explanation for inspection, keeping educational interpretation separate from a recommendation to trade.

paragraphs: An AI model can sound careful without knowing how reliable its answer is. I try to keep that difference clear. A useful summary should say when information is missing and avoid giving a made-up sense of certainty.
1.title: Uncertainty Without Invented Precision

paragraphs: New data gives the model different material to work with, but it can still explain that material badly. I need to check both how fresh the inputs are and whether the summary matches them.
3.title: Fresh Inputs Do Not Guarantee Better Reasoning

2.title: Building the Backend
items: I used FastAPI to connect data requests, calculations, and AI responses.
Docker packages the application and its dependencies for deployment.
Keeping these steps separate helps me track where an incorrect summary began.

0.intro: Working on the explanations meant learning what the financial terms actually describe:

items.label: Pricing concepts
items.body: Distinguish an observed price from an estimate produced under a model’s assumptions.

items.label: Sensitivity measures
items.body: Delta, gamma, theta, and vega describe different quantities, not interchangeable indicators of risk.

items.label: Market context
items.body: Spread, liquidity, and timing affect interpretation.

items.label: Risk descriptions
items.body: A qualitative risk explanation is separate from a tested portfolio-risk model.

paragraphs: Using a technical term correctly matters more than simply including it. I want a reader to be able to connect an explanation back to the number or calculation it describes.

1.title: Information-Quality Checks
1.intro: Evaluation should examine the transformation from data to explanation:
items: Check whether descriptions match the values actually supplied.
Identify unsupported causal claims, forecasts, and omitted limitations.
Separate missing or delayed data from a genuine absence of activity.
Test comprehensibility without implying guaranteed outcomes.

2.title: Checks Before Trusting a Summary
2.intro: A useful explanation should make these details easy to check:

items.label: Source
items.body: Which market data and time period does it use?

items.label: Calculation
items.body: Do the inputs and assumptions match the measure being described?

items.label: Explanation
items.body: Does the model’s wording match the numbers?

items.label: Missing information
items.body: Does the summary say when a source is delayed or unavailable?

0.title: What I Want Readers to Be Able to Do

items.label: Comprehensibility
items.body: Make unfamiliar measures easier to explore without replacing definitions with oversimplified claims.

items.label: Transparency
items.body: Distinguish a source observation from a model’s interpretation.

items.label: Critical reading
items.body: Help readers question a summary rather than treat fluency as proof.

1.title: Questions for Further Evaluation
1.intro: These are questions I use to review the explanations:

items.label: Checking the numbers
items.body: Does the summary describe the numbers I actually gave the model?

items.label: Checking the wording
items.body: Does the wording make the result sound more certain than the evidence allows?

items.label: Tracing a sentence to its source
items.body: Can a reader check which data or calculation a sentence came from?

items.label: Making it understandable
items.body: Can I explain a difficult idea clearly while keeping the important assumptions visible?

paragraphs: I built the path from external data to an AI-written explanation, including the backend and interactive CFO insight agents. Reaching 1,000+ Google Search Console clicks by October 2026 showed that people were finding the site through search. It did not tell me whether they understood every explanation; that needs a different kind of evaluation.
2.title: My Contribution and the Site’s Reach

paragraphs: Zeitgeist gave me practice building a pipeline from external data to an AI-generated explanation. My work included data ingestion, the FastAPI backend, and the model integration.

Each step has different things to check: whether data arrived, whether a calculation used the right inputs, and whether the explanation matches those inputs. A summary can read well even when one of those steps has gone wrong. I want a reader to be able to check an explanation against the numbers behind it.

The project made me more interested in how people read unfamiliar information. Writing an explanation is easy for a model; helping someone check it against its source is a harder problem I want to keep working on.

elocutionist.title: Elocutionist — Speaking & Interview Practice
subtitles: Interview practice with AI questions and feedback

paragraphs: Elocutionist is an independent app I built for interview practice. It lets a user add background information, answer questions by typing or speaking, and review AI-generated feedback.
My work included the application, document processing, speech transcription, and feedback system. It was separate from the interview module I worked on with a team at DreamCollege.ai.

items.title: Add background
items.body: The app reads background information and document text to create relevant questions.

items.title: Capture a response
items.body: Users type or record an answer. Whisper turns the recording into text for the feedback step.

items.title: Generate feedback
items.body: The model returns suggestions about the answer’s content and structure. Users decide which suggestions fit.

items.title: Review and practice again
items.body: Users can play back recordings and revisit earlier answers before trying again.

paragraphs: I added interactive 3D interviewer avatars, drawing inspiration from Proxona, as another way to practice alongside text and voice. I would need user testing to know whether they make practice more effective.
1.title: Trying a 3D Interviewer

Human-AI Interaction Design.heading: Helping the Speaker Stay in Control

items.label: The speaker’s own words
items.body: Give users room to answer in their own words before offering suggestions.

items.label: Relevant questions
items.body: Use the background they provide to ask relevant questions, while allowing for mistakes in reading the documents.

items.label: Specific suggestions
items.body: Explain which part of an answer could be clearer so the speaker can decide whether the suggestion fits.

items.label: Looking back at an answer
items.body: Let users revisit their responses and recordings. Treat the AI score as one piece of feedback.

paragraphs: Building Elocutionist gave me practice connecting several parts of an application: reading background documents, generating questions, transcribing an answer, and returning feedback. A problem in an early step can affect what comes after it.

I worked on turning the model’s response into suggestions about the answer’s content and structure. The transcript gives the model words to work with, but it leaves out parts of how someone speaks. I wanted the suggestions to give users something to consider while letting them decide how to revise their own answers.

This was independent development. DreamCollege gave me a different setting, where I had to connect my work to other developers’ work and to an existing product. The two projects gave me practice with both ways of building software.
